name: Tumbuka
confidence_why: Downing's first-hand work (2006, 2019) shows that the penult lengthening and High tone appear only on the phrase-final word, so the phrase-level reading is well supported, but it rests on a single fieldworker, and Vail (1972) and Kisseberth & Odden (2003), known here only through Downing's own citations, label the same penult prominence as word-level stress.

That is, penult lengthening and a High tone on the initial mora of the lengthened penult are phrase-level properties, not word-level ones, as only some words in a sentence have this prosody. Instead, it could be considered a correlate of phrasal stress – that is, intonational level pitch-accent – as High tones consistently occur on the first mora of penult syllables that are lengthened as another correlate of phrasal stress. ... For these reasons, Kisseberth & Odden (2003) and Vail (1972) classify Tumbuka as a stress language, suggesting…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Tumbuka (tumb1250) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Downing 2006 (ZASPiL 43), was downloaded open access and read: it is first-hand fieldwork and states that Chitumbuka has no lexical tone contrasts and that every word in isolation lengthens its penult and bears a falling H tone, with the H 'aligned with the stressed penult' (pp. 57-58); fn. 1 records that Kisseberth & Odden 2003 classify the language as a stress language while Downing calls the system more tone-like (predictable pitch accent). Two further first-hand Downing papers were obtained and read (2008 ZASPiL 49, already held by the project from the Zulu download; 2012 ACAL 42 from lingref) and restate fixed penult lengthening as the correlate of phrasal and sentence stress, not moved by focus. Chavula 2016 (LOT 423, native speaker) says Citumbuka is not tonal and notes penultimate stress as a cue in intensive vs causative suffixes but gives no placement rule. Elmslie 1891 (archive.org) is silent. Unread: Downing 2010 'Accent in African languages' (De Gruyter, paywalled; medium priority), Kisseberth & Odden 2003 (print), Kiso 2012 (DiVA unreachable), Young 1932 (no open copy; Recommended coding for a new catalog record: fixed penultimate prominence (length + falling tone), no lexical tone; classification as stress vs predictable pitch accent is contested in the source itself. new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (20 pp., text layer, Language Science Press CC-BY, pp. 75-94) with extracted text. All three quoted passages are present verbatim at the stated locators. p. 76 (§2.1 'Words in isolation – non-ideophones'): 'there are no lexical or grammatical tonal contrasts in the non-ideophonic lexicon of Tumbuka.. Vowel length is also not contrastive: the penult of every word in isolation is lengthened and its first half bears a High tone', followed by noun/verb lists (múu-nthu, ku-líima, ŵa-ka-mu-zengeráa-ni) with penult H on lengthened penult throughout. p. 78 (§2.2 'Tumbuka phrasal prosody'): 'Tumbuka words have the isolation pronunciation illustrated in (1) and (2) only when they are final in…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Prominence (vowel lengthening plus a High tone on the first mora, i.e. a falling contour) sits on the penultimate syllable of the last word of each Phonological Phrase; a word pronounced in isolation therefore shows penultimate prominence, but phrase-medial words have neither lengthening nor the falling tone. Downing treats this as phrasal stress / intonational pitch accent and denies word-level stress; Vail (1972) and Kisseberth & Odden (2003), as reported by Downing, treat the same facts as a penultimate stress language that has lost Proto-Bantu tone. If the catalog wants a word-level value for citation forms, it is penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described. Downing 2019 Table 1 (p. 83) leaves the 'privative' (no secondary stress) property marked '?' for Tumbuka at phrase level; no secondary stress is mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Ideophones carry contrastive level High and Low tones and do not take the penult falling contour (Downing 2019 §2.3 pp. 79-80, after Vail 1972, Mphande 1989; Moto 1999). Sentence-final (Intonational Phrase-final) penults get extra lengthening = culminative sentence stress (Downing 2006 p. 59; 2012 p. 126). Chavula 2016 notes the intensive suffix -ísk- bears accent on its vowel, unlike causative -isk-. Yes-no questions add a High-Low fall on the final syllable (Downing 2008).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological Phrase (right edge of XP): only phrase-final words show penult lengthening + H; citation forms (words in isolation) are phrase-final and so show penultimate prominence. Downing explicitly frames the system as phrase-level, not word-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Downing's data are from fieldwork with Malawian Tumbuka speakers (consultants via the Centre for Language Studies, University of Malawi; Bantu N.21); no dialect is specified. Chavula 2016 is also Malawian Citumbuka. No separate glottocode issue; tumb1250 as targeted.

new_statements.quote: there are no lexical or grammatical tonal contrasts in Chitumbuka. The penult of every word in isolation is lengthened and bears a falling tone [...] In sum, the word-level tone system of Chitumbuka has many defining properties of a pitch-accent language (Downing 2003, to appear; Hyman 1977; Odden 1999): obligatoriness and culminativity: every word has one and only one High tone; positional restrictions: only the penult can bear a High tone; and tone-stress interaction: the High tone aligns with the stressed penult.
new_statements.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2006. The prosody and syntax of focus in Chitumbuka. ZAS Papers in Linguistics 43: 55-79. doi:10.21248/zaspil.43.2006.285
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.1 'Words in isolation', pp. 57-58 (with fn. 1, p. 58)
new_statements.reading: Fixed penultimate word prominence: every word in isolation has a lengthened penult carrying a falling (H) tone, with no lexical tone contrasts; phrase-medially the lengthening is lost. Kisseberth & Odden 2003 call this a stress language (fixed penult); Downing prefers to call it a predictable pitch accent system that is 'more tone-like than stress-like'. Either way the placement is fixed on the penult, with culminative extra lengthening on the sentence-final penult. First-hand fieldwork data.

new_statements.quote: "Stress-accent is widely reported for languages from all over the Bantu-speaking area. Some of the earliest work on Bantu prosody, like Werner (1919), observes that the penult syllable is the most likely to be stressed. The table below, which lists a geographically diverse set of Bantu languages, shows that this is indeed the overwhelmingly most common pattern: (15) Summary table of stress-accent in Bantu languages | Language | Stress position | Tone? | Source | ... Tumbuka | penult | no | Odden 1999" [p. 121]. "The most commonly reported phonetic correlate of penult stress, for both the tonal and non-tonal languages listed above, is vowel lengthening, with sources often noting that lengthening is most noticeable when words are in phrase-final position." [p. 122]

Page 22 (= p. 122) has verbatim…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement (penult) as the existing Downing 2006 statement and as Kisseberth & Odden 2003 (cited there); classifies Tumbuka as a non-tonal penult stress-accent language. It treats the penult prominence as word-level stress-accent, which the existing Downing 2019 statement (phrase-level prominence only, 'no word level stress properties') explicitly revises; so it agrees on placement and differs from Downing 2019 on the domain (word vs phrase). It is a secondary-source table entry (citing Odden 1999), not first-hand data. The catalog record's rule field is currently empty; this source supports filling it as fixed penult.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Survey-table entry only: Tumbuka is listed among Bantu languages with penultimate stress-accent and no tone, on the authority of Odden 1999 (Typological issues in tone and stress in Bantu). The general discussion adds that the phonetic correlate of Bantu penult stress is vowel lengthening, most noticeable phrase-finally. No Tumbuka data, no dialect, and no further discussion of Tumbuka anywhere else in the paper (single mention).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Tumbuka. The paper's general remark that penult lengthening is most noticeable in phrase-final position is the same fact Downing 2019 later uses to argue the prominence is phrasal rather than word-level.
new_statements.identity_note: Downing 2004/2010 lists 'Tumbuka' with no dialect or location. The first-hand sources already held by the project (Downing 2006, 2019) describe Tumbuka N.21 of northern Malawi from the author's own fieldwork; Chavula 2016 (held by the project) is on Citumbuka of Malawi and states it is not a tonal language. No source opened describes a divergent variety.

readall_conflicts: Placement is uncontested: every source opened (Downing 2004/2010 survey table citing Odden 1999; Downing 2006 first-hand; Downing 2019 first-hand; Vail 1972 and Kisseberth & Odden 2003 as cited by Downing) puts the prominence (lengthening plus High tone) on the penult, and all agree Tumbuka has no lexical tone contrasts. The disagreement is about the level and type: Downing 2004/2010, Kisseberth & Odden 2003 and Vail 1972 call it (word-level) penultimate stress in a non-tonal language; Downing 2006 calls it a predictable pitch accent system 'more tone-like than stress-like'; Downing 2019 argues penult lengthening and H are phrase-level properties (only phrase-final words show them) so that 'Tumbuka actually has no word level stress properties' and it is 'at best a non-canonical stress language'. Downing 2004/2010's own remark that Bantu penult lengthening is most noticeable phrase-finally is consistent with that later analysis. Kiso 2012 could not be opened, so its position is unknown.

sources.quote: Citumbuka is not a tonal language. It has five vowels and all of them are short in quality [...] (p. 11) — There are two major differences between the intensive and causative in Citumbuka. Firstly, the intensive does not introduce a new argument; and secondly, the penultimate syllable is more stressed in an intensive than a causative. In this thesis, the intensive suffix is therefore, presented as -ísk/ésk- (p. 155)
sources.note: Native-speaker morphosyntax thesis; no phonology sketch of stress placement (the author recommends a phonology study, p. 226). States that Citumbuka is not tonal and notes penultimate stress as the cue distinguishing intensive -ísk- from causative -isk-, which presupposes penultimate prominence but gives no general placement rule.

[...] penult lengthening is considered the principal correlate of phrasal and sentential stress prominence in Tumbuka.

sources.quote: In all three languages, lengthening of the phrase penult syllable is the easiest to identify – and most consistent – correlate of prosodic phrasing. [...] In all three of these Bantu languages, though, the highest degree of stress (defined as vowel lengthening) in the sentence is fixed on the penult syllable of the final prosodic phrase in the sentence. [...] phrase stress falls consistently on the phrase penult syllable.
sources.note: Phrasal stress = lengthening of phrase-penult syllables in all three languages; sentence-final phrase penult is longest (culminative sentence stress); stress fixed phrase-finally and utterance-finally, not moved by focus (sections 2.2, 3.1-3.2).
